name: apkid
desc: Android application identifier for compilers, packers, and obfuscators
why: Identifies which compilers, packers and obfuscators built an Android APK, a good window into how apps get wrapped.

brief.what_it_is: APKiD is a command-line tool that reports how an Android APK was built and protected. It takes an APK, a DEX file, or a directory as input (a FILE argument, optionally recursive) and scans it with YARA rules. It outputs which compilers, packers, obfuscators, and other notable traits it recognizes, per classes.dex entry, either as text or as JSON (-j), or written to a directory with -o. The README's example output shows a line like ' |-> compiler : dx'. It is written in Python and installs from PyPI.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says APKiD 'gives you information about how an APK was made' and calls it 'PEiD for Android', after the Windows tool that identified packers and compilers in PE executables. The author also points to detecting pirated and malicious apps and to fingerprinting AppShielding and mobile RASP SDKs.
brief.how_it_works: It applies a set of YARA rules to APK and DEX contents to match signatures of known compilers, packers, and obfuscators. The README says new detections are added as rules, and the Hacking section says the rules must be compiled with prep-release.py before they take effect. The README does not describe the matching internals beyond this.

brief.install_notes: The README's primary route is pip install apkid. Docker is an alternative: it requires git and Docker, and the README says to clone the repo and build the image locally. For development, clone the repo, install yara-python and yara-python-dex, run python prep-release.py to compile the rules, then pip install -e .[dev,test]. On Windows, the README asks for removing other YARA versions, pinning yara-python 3.11.0, and building yara-python-dex from the MobSF git repo. The README's sample Docker output says 'APKiD 2.1.0' while its usage text says v2.1.2, so the README is not fully consistent on version numbers. No accounts or hardware are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is explicitly modelled on PEiD, applied to Android, and its rule set is extensible. The README invites issues for unrecognized files and encourages contributions beyond packers, including anti-disassembler and anti-VM tricks, so it works as a catalogue of how apps are wrapped and not only as a compiler detector.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a Travis CI badge, a PyPI badge, and a usage text at version 2.1.2, and it cites a BlackHat USA 2023 Arsenal talk, which suggests activity into 2023. The fetched README gives no release date or last commit, and I did not fetch the PyPI or commit history to confirm.
brief.caveats: The README's Windows instructions are involved and depend on a specific yara-python version and a git-hosted yara-python-dex build. Development setup needs yara-python and yara-python-dex installed before prep-release.py will work. Licensing is dual: a commercial license for closed-source use and GPL for open-source use, so the user must choose one. Detection is only as good as the rule set: unknown packers show up as unrecognized until someone submits a sample.

entry.title: APKiD
entry.tldr: PEiD for Android: point it at an APK and it reports which compilers, packers and obfuscators were used to build and wrap the app.
entry.deeper_look:
APKiD takes an APK, a DEX file, or a directory and scans the contents with YARA rules. For each classes.dex it reports what it recognizes, such as the compiler (the README's example prints `|-> compiler : dx`), packers, obfuscators, and other traits. Output is plain text, JSON with `-j`, or files in a directory with `-o`.

The README describes it as "PEiD for Android", after the Windows tool that identified packers and compilers in PE executables. The author's stated uses are spotting pirated and malicious apps and fingerprinting AppShielding and mobile RASP SDKs.

The idea underneath is that an app is rarely shipped as it was compiled. Build tools leave marks, and protection tools leave their own. Matching those marks with signature rules shows how an app was wrapped before you open a disassembler. It also shows which protections you are about to run into.

The rule set is meant to grow. The README invites issues for unrecognized files and asks for ideas beyond packers, including anti-disassembler and anti-VM tricks. That makes the rules a small catalogue of how apps defend themselves.
entry.install:
brew install apkid
# Needs an Android APK or DEX file to scan. No account or hardware. Also available via `pip install apkid`.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the usage text: scan depth, timeout, recursion, typing mode, and JSON output options.
Scans the APK and prints the compilers, packers and obfuscators it recognizes for each classes.dex.
Prints the same findings as JSON, which is easier to feed into scripts.

entry.whats_unique: It is modelled directly on PEiD and driven by YARA rules anyone can extend, so it works as a catalogue of how Android apps get wrapped, not only a compiler detector.
entry.caveats: Detection is only as good as the rule set, so unknown packers go unrecognized until someone submits a sample, and the project's current maintenance status is unclear from the README.
